paper.abstract: Abstract Agentic stock prediction systems make sequences of interdependent decisions (regime detection, pathway routing, reinforcement learning control) whose individual quality is hidden by aggregate metrics such as mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) or directional accuracy. We present a behavioral evaluation framework that addresses this gap. Behavioral traces logged at every autonomous decision point are grouped into five-day episodes and scored along six domain-specific dimensions (regime detection, routing, adaptation, risk calibration, strategy coherence, error recovery) by an ensemble of three large language model (LLM) judges (GPT 5.4, Claude 4.6 Opus, Gemini 3.1 Pro). Perturbation-based validation on 420 episodes yields targeted score drops of − 1.6 -1.6 to − 2.4 -2.4 on intended dimensions versus an average of − 0.32 -0.32 on the remaining five, with cross-model agreement up to Krippendorff’s α = 0.85 \alpha=0.85 . The composite behavioral score, used here only for cross-episode reporting, correlates at ρ = 0.72 \rho=0.72 with realized 20-day Sharpe ratio from offline backtesting. Closing the loop, the framework converts deficient per-dimension scores into a credit-assigned penalty term added to the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) reward. Three short fine-tuning cycles, all confined to the validation period, produce on the held-out 2017–2025 test period a one-day MAPE reduction from 0.61% to 0.54% (an 11.5% relative reduction; p < 0.001 p<0.001 , Cohen’s d = 0.31 d=0.31 ), a directional accuracy increase from 71% to 74%, and an 18% Sharpe ratio improvement (95% bootstrap CI [8.2%, 27.4%]), with gains concentrated in high-volatility episodes where the original system was most behaviorally deficient. Results are from offline backtesting and do not address effects specific to live deployment.

Index Terms: LLM-as-a-Judge, evaluation, agents, reinforcement, prediction, credit-assignment, backtesting. I Introduction Modern stock prediction systems increasingly behave as agents in the operational sense that they perform sequences of autonomous decisions on every trading day, combining learned regime detection, pathway routing, and a reinforcement learning controller [ 1 ] . The quality of such agents is almost universally summarized through aggregate output metrics (MAPE, RMSE, directional accuracy, Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown), which capture what the system produced but reveal nothing about whether the intermediate decisions that produced it were sound. An agent may arrive at a correct forecast through unsound routing, or produce an incorrect forecast despite making prudent regime and risk-calibration choices. Aggregate scores conflate these cases, yet distinguishing them is essential for diagnosing failures, calibrating trust, and guiding further improvement [ 2 , 3 ] . The LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm has been shown to produce evaluations that align closely with human raters on natural-language tasks [ 4 , 5 ] , and those judgments are reliable enough to drive downstream optimization in language model alignment [ 6 , 7 ] . Most existing applications evaluate static outputs (single responses, summaries, dialogue turns). Evaluating an autonomous prediction system instead requires assessing temporal sequences of interdependent decisions made under stochastic conditions, where the same decision may be appropriate under one regime and inappropriate under another, and where decision quality cannot always be inferred from immediate outcomes due to market noise [ 8 ] . To the best of our knowledge, the present work is the first systematic application of structured LLM-based behavioral evaluation, with rubric-anchored multi-dimensional scoring, to autonomous stock prediction systems with closed-loop reinforcement learning integration; we do not claim priority on LLM-based evaluation in general, nor on other financial forecasting settings. This Short Communication presents the framework and applies it to the adaptive regime-aware prediction system from [ 1 ] . Three contributions are made. First, multi-step decision evaluation is formalized through structured behavioral traces and six domain-specific dimensions that decompose behavioral quality into separately assessable components. Second, a perturbation-based validation methodology is introduced, with each perturbation engineered to corrupt one dimension while leaving the other five mechanically intact, so that the responsiveness of dimension scores to targeted degradation can be measured directly. Third, a credit-assignment mechanism translates per-dimension diagnostics into targeted modifications of the SAC reward, allowing the existing reinforcement learning controller to correct identified weaknesses without changes to the underlying architecture. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II positions the work relative to prior LLM evaluation, agent assessment, and financial AI evaluation. Section III describes the framework. Section IV reports validation, predictive-validity, and closed-loop results. Section V discusses interpretation and limitations. Section VI concludes. II Related Work The LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm has been shown to align with human evaluation on natural-language tasks [ 4 , 5 ] and to support reward-model training in RLHF [ 7 , 6 ] . These applications evaluate single static outputs rather than temporal sequences of interdependent decisions. In parallel, the agent-evaluation literature has produced reasoning-trace frameworks (ReAct [ 9 ] , Reflexion [ 10 ] ) that externalize agent decision-making, but assessment in those frameworks remains tied to binary task success, leaving process-quality evaluation an open problem [ 3 , 8 ] . In financial AI, evaluation continues to be dominated by aggregate output metrics whose distributions cannot localize which intermediate component failed or why [ 2 , 11 , 12 ] . The present work addresses both gaps in a coupled way by adapting LLM-as-a-Judge to temporal financial decision sequences with domain-specific dimensions, and by routing the resulting per-dimension diagnostics into the SAC reward through a credit-assignment mechanism so that evaluation is no longer purely passive but actively corrective during fine-tuning. III Behavioral Evaluation Framework III-A Agent and behavioral trace The evaluation framework is developed for the adaptive regime-aware prediction system of [ 1 ] , which processes daily data for 20 S&P 500 equities (January 1982 to March 2025) using an autoencoder for regime detection, dual node-transformer pathways [ 13 ] specialized for stable and volatile conditions, and a Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) reinforcement learning controller [ 14 ] that adaptively tunes the regime detection threshold τ \tau and the pathway blending weight α t \alpha_{t} . The system performs four autonomous decisions each day: (i) the autoencoder computes reconstruction error e t = ‖ x t − x ^ t ‖ 2 e_{t}=\|x_{t}-\hat{x}_{t}\|_{2} and emits a regime label ℓ t ∈ { 0 , 1 } \ell_{t}\in\{0,1\} by comparing e t e_{t} to τ \tau ; (ii) a router selects the normal or event pathway; (iii) the system blends y ^ t = α t ​ y normal + ( 1 − α t ) ​ y event \hat{y}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\,y_{\text{normal}}+(1-\alpha_{t})\,y_{\text{event}} ; and (iv) the SAC controller adjusts both τ \tau and α t \alpha_{t} . All experiments report offline backtesting on historical equity data; effects specific to live deployment (latency, slippage, market impact) are outside the scope of this work. A structured behavioral trace is logged at every trading day: ℬ t = ⟨ 𝐦 t , 𝐚 t , 𝐫 t , 𝐮 t , y ^ t , 𝐩 t ⟩ , \mathcal{B}_{t}=\langle\,\mathbf{m}_{t},\;\mathbf{a}_{t},\;\mathbf{r}_{t},\;\mathbf{u}_{t},\;\hat{y}_{t},\;\mathbf{p}_{t}\,\rangle, (1) where 𝐦 t = ( p t , v t , VIX t , S ¯ t ) \mathbf{m}_{t}=(p_{t},v_{t},\mathrm{VIX}_{t},\bar{S}_{t}) is the market context (price, volume, volatility index, BERT sentiment), 𝐚 t = ( e t , τ t , ℓ t ) \mathbf{a}_{t}=(e_{t},\tau_{t},\ell_{t}) is the autoencoder output, 𝐫 t = ( α t , k t ) \mathbf{r}_{t}=(\alpha_{t},k_{t}) is the routing decision, 𝐮 t = ( Δ ​ τ t , Δ ​ α t ) ∈ [ − 0.1 , 0.1 ] 2 \mathbf{u}_{t}=(\Delta\tau_{t},\Delta\alpha_{t})\in[-0.1,0.1]^{2} is the SAC action, and 𝐩 t \mathbf{p}_{t} is a 20-day rolling (MAPE, DA) summary. Five consecutive traces form an evaluation episode ℰ t = { ℬ t , … , ℬ t + 4 } \mathcal{E}_{t}=\{\mathcal{B}_{t},\ldots,\mathcal{B}_{t+4}\} . The five-day window provides enough temporal context to assess adaptation and recovery while remaining within a single market regime, and matches the SAC controller’s own state-history length. Episodes are sampled without overlap to reduce statistical dependence between evaluated units. III-B Six evaluation dimensions Each episode is scored on six dimensions chosen to cover both individual architectural decisions and emergent system-level behaviors (Table I ). The first three (Regime Detection, Routing, Adaptation) map directly to specific decision points and assess whether each component performed its designated function. The remaining three (Risk Calibration, Strategy Coherence, Error Recovery) are emergent properties that depend on the interaction of multiple components and cannot be attributed to any single subsystem. Error Recovery in particular is anchored to a precise event detector, ξ t = [ MAPE t > MAPE ¯ t , 20 + σ MAPE , t , 20 ] , \xi_{t}\;=\;\mathbb{1}\!\left[\,\mathrm{MAPE}_{t}\;>\;\overline{\mathrm{MAPE}}_{t,20}\,+\,\sigma_{\mathrm{MAPE},t,20}\,\right], (2) where MAPE ¯ t , 20 \overline{\mathrm{MAPE}}_{t,20} and σ MAPE , t , 20 \sigma_{\mathrm{MAPE},t,20} are the rolling mean and standard deviation of daily MAPE over the preceding 20 trading days; episodes with ξ t = 1 \xi_{t}=1 are scored on whether the SAC controller produces a measurable corrective adjustment within two trading days. Each dimension is scored on a 1–5 Likert scale with anchored rubric descriptions; a 1–5 scale was adopted because preliminary experiments with a 1–10 scale yielded lower inter-judge agreement without additional diagnostic content.
